utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody in the court. May the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, please, beginning with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis and Aditya Menon for the Prosecution, assisted by our case manager Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the Prosecution, to everyone in and around the courtroom. I am Vasvija Vidovic representing General Rasim Delic, with my case manager Lana Deljkic, legal assistant Sabina Dzubur, and with the help of legal assistant from OKO, Nina Kisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Sir, before we start, may you sit for a while, please. Just to -- to put on the record that this session of this trial is sitting in Sarajevo pursuant to Rule 4 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia, and Mr. -- may we then ask the witness to please make the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, can you please state your full name, spelling both your first and last names, please.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: First I would like to say my name is Ajman, A-j-m-a-n, and mine last name is Awad, A-w-a-d. I would like to say that I was summoned here to testify at the request of the Prosecution not versus or against Rasim Delic but in the case of Rasim Delic, and it's not a fact that I voluntarily came to testify but that I'm here to testify on the basis of your summons and request. I would like this to be noted in the record. They said that I was representative of the Ensario [phoen] Association and to testify on their behalf. I'm not testifying on their behalf. I would just like to say that I am here testifying at the request of The Hague Prosecution or Prosecutor's office today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, bearing in mind what the witness has just said, may I just remind the parties that should there be any private sessions that the parties would like us to go into, can we please try to do that either at the beginning or at the end of the testimony so that we don't interrupt the public gallery, because we would have to clear the public gallery when we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, can you please state your date and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I was born on the 1st of April, 1964, in Syria.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell the Trial Chamber of which country or countries are you currently a citizen?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Currently I have the citizenship of the Arab Republic of Syria, because my BH citizenship was revoked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, can you please tell us when you first came to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I came in 1982 to Belgrade. From Belgrade I went to Zagreb where I stayed and enrolled in university. After Zagreb, I transferred to another town, Rijeka, where I remind for seven years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, during the time period that you were in Croatia, what subject or subjects did you study?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I studied medicine, and because of certain circumstances, because of financial matters, I stopped studying there and went to study physiotherapy, but I did not graduate. I only had four exams left, and I stopped my studies there in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, sir, what language you studied medicine and physiotherapy in?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Then it was called Croato-Serbian, Hrvatsko-Sprski language.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, how did you come to learn how to speak that language?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: When I came to Zagreb, I enrolled at the faculty of philosophy, the department for language studies, and I went to a course for six months and I received a diploma which I could then use to enroll at the medical faculty because I knew Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where were you, Mr. Awad, when the war began in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I was in Croatia, in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did there come a time, sir, when you left Rijeka and went to Bosnia and Herzegovina in the early part of the war?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Not at the beginning of the war, but in late 1992 I came to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, a few moments ago, sir, I believe, at least the English translation you said you left Croatia in 1994. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I didn't say the number 4. I said I was born in 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Just to avoid any confusion, then, Mr. Awad, when did you leave Croatia in order to go to Bosnia? What time period? What month and year?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: In December 1992, in late December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, a little bit about the circumstances under which you went to Bosnia in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Are you talking about my reasons for coming to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's start with -- let's start with that question, sir. What were the reasons why you came to Bosnia and Herzegovina in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I came intending to fight in Bosnia and Herzegovina on the side of Bosnian Muslims. After I worked for a brief period in Rijeka in receiving refugees and helping refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, when I heard their stories and what suffering they went through and humiliation, I decided that somebody else could do the work in the humanitarian organisation and that I, as an able-bodied Muslim man could contribute more by helping the people, these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, when you say the "humanitarian organisation," do you remember the name of the humanitarian organisation that you were working with in Rijeka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: There was several organisations. We were just coordinating the humanitarian organisations. There was Igasa, Appeal International, Islamic Relief, even Merhamet that was founded there, and we cooperated with them and helped them in their work. In late 1992, I joined the Mowafaq Foundation, humanitarian organisation, and that is the organisation I was a member of when I entered Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. Awad, if you're able to do so, can you please spell the name of the Mowafaq Foundation?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: M-w -- actually, before that it's o-w-a-f-a-q.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we get that spelling again in English from the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: M-o-w-a-f-a-q.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And while we're on that point, is there a way in which we can get the interpretation on the screens or is there no way?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I don't believe that's possible, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. You may proceed, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, can you tell us how your trip to Bosnia and Herzegovina in December 1992 was organised?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The director of the organisation asked those of us who wanted to work in Bosnia and Herzegovina to go. He actually asked us, actually myself and two of my colleagues, to enter Bosnia and Herzegovina to gather information about what were the things that were essential, most needed for assistance at that point. I went -- or, actually, we set out from Zagreb. We went to Split, and then from Split we came by car from somebody from Visoko, and that person took us to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were your intentions upon arriving in Zenica? What exactly was it, sir, that you expected to be doing after arriving in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Since the director asked us to collect information about what was most needed, the first thing was to visit the different authorities, the different bodies who were responsible for this, to get direct information from them. And then I need to explain immediately this, why I came to the Mowafaq Foundation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Before that I was in contact with another organisation. It was Benevolence International, which already had training places in Bosnia and Herzegovina for Bosnian soldiers. I wanted to come to Bosnia to fight, and then I thought I could use that opportunity and help with translation, because I knew I spoke Bosnian or Croato-Serbian, which was spoken before. So to help with translation, interpreting, and also help in fighting in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did you go or where were you staying when you arrived in Zenica in December 1992?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Late December, so then we now already moved into 1993. January 1993 I was in Zenica staying at the Metalurg Hotel, and then later I asked for better accommodation so that you don't have to pay 10 marks every day. Then they found an apartment where we could live for a whole months for a hundred or a hundred and fifty marks, and that's where we were staying in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Awad, when you say "we," can you tell us who you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I'm referring to the team that came with me, those two men, the two colleagues to came with me from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall their names?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: One was Edib [phoen], and the other one was Basar [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, where these two individuals, Edib and Basar, were from?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Edib was a Palestinian who was living in Bosnia and Herzegovina for a while, and Basar was a colleague of mine from Syria who studied medicine with me in Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, you told us that it was your intention to fight. That was the reason you came to Bosnia. Sir, in fact did there come a time in 1993 when you joined a military unit or fighting force?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: In 1993, in April, I joined a group of Arab Mujahedin who were accommodated in Bilmiste. That's where the -- the 7th Muslim Brigade barracks was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At that point in time, sir, April 1993, how big was in group of foreign or Arab Mujahedin who were accommodated at Bilmiste barracks in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: There were eight to ten people accommodated there. There weren't more than that. Eight to ten people who were staying in two rooms. One was on the ground floor, which was used as a kitchen for cooking, also for the wounded and so on, and on the first floor there was a classroom where the others slept. I think it was ten people. Not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall where these ten people were from, what country or countries?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Some were from Libya, Algiers -- Algeria, Morocco, Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon. That's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, if one person from amongst this group was in charge of the group?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Each group usually has someone who's responsible for the group. In this situation Abu Mali was in charge -- in charge of those people in that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where was Abu Mali from?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Abu Mali was from Algeria.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the name or names of any of the other foreign Mujahedin who were with you in Bilmiste barracks in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Ajub [phoen] from Morocco was there, Abu Hamza from Jordan, Abu Talib from Lebanon, Abu Mali. Before that I had met Dr. Abu Haris, but he wasn't staying there at those premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who was Dr. Abu Haris, and where was he from?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Abu Haris was from Libya. For a certain period of time he was the emir of the El Mujahedin Detachment -- or, rather, the commander of the El Mujahedin Detachment or those Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, we'll talk about the El Mujahedin Detachment a little bit later this morning. I'd like to focus your attention at this time on the period April 1993. This group of foreign Mujahedin who were accommodated at Bilmiste barracks in Zenica, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: They didn't have any activities. They were just staying there. They didn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Based on -- well, let me ask you this, sir: How long approximately did you remain at Bilmiste barracks? How long were you accommodated there?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: For two months almost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During this two-month period, Mr. Awad, or shortly less than two-month period, did you have the opportunity to learn anything about the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I didn't inquire or speak to people, so not much of that really interested me. I didn't ask about it except that they were just billeted there as a force. I knew that the commander was Amir Kubura. Halil Brzina was also there. I think he was in charge of logistics. Mahmut Karalic was there as emir. They referred to him as emir. I think also Ahmed Adilovic was there. He was in charge of morale. I think it was morale. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, us just told us that Halil Brzina, you thought, was in charge of logistics. What gave you that impression, or why did you come to understand or believe that Mr. Brzina was in charge of logistics for the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I received the first uniform that I wore in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Awad, approximately when Mr. Brzina provided you with this army uniform?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: This was in April 1993. Before that I dropped by there as a humanitarian person, a person who came with a humanitarian organisation, and we met some people there and so on. An incident happened. There was an event in Zenica, and people -- joint patrols of the HVO and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina military police, joint patrols came out into the streets, and one night I could not get to the apartment where I was staying. The reason for that was the blockades. And I think there was a kidnapping that happened in Zenica then. Since I couldn't get to my apartment, and I was quite insulted by members of the HVO, and the Bosnian military police couldn't defend me from them, I threatened that I would press charges against them since I was a member of a humanitarian organisation and they couldn't treat me like that, but they wouldn't let me go to my apartment. And from that time, I came back, and then I joined that group of Arabs, because the next day -- or in two days the conflict broke out in Zenica. At the time it was a conflict between the Bosnia and Herzegovina army and the HVO, and the fighting was being waged in the area of Podbrezje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'll -- we'll turn to some of this fighting between the army and the HVO in just a moment, but I'd like to return to this uniform that you were provided with. Do you recall -- can you describe what this uniform looked like?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: An ordinary uniform. The top part, somebody calls it a blouse, somebody a jacket, and trousers. That was what I was given. Since I was in civilian clothes, I asked to have something of military dress so that I would look like a military man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness may have mentioned this earlier when he referred to the uniform. I just wanted to make sure that it's there on the record. Of which army was this uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether they had special uniforms, the uniforms worn by the people in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. All the soldiers wore uniforms. Whether it was the HVO or the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they all wore similar uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Here you say whether it was the HVO or the army of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they wore similar uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you by that to be saying that the uniform of the HVO and the uniform of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was exactly the same?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For me it was the same. I didn't make any distinction. When I saw those men at the HVO check-point, I saw that they were wearing a similar uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when they were in combat, how did they distinguish each other? Surely if two armies that are at war with each other are wearing exactly the same type of uniform, they may -- you may find that there's a lot of friendly fire.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could have happened, but what I saw, what I noticed at first glance when I came there, I saw that the uniforms were similar. Now, if we're talking about the next stage of the fighting, certain insignia were worn. There may be a ribbon on the left or right shoulder. The warring parties were not attacking from the same positions. For example, if Vitez is attacked where HVO was stationed, then they wouldn't be attacked from the side where the HVO but, rather, where the lines of the BH army was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did you have any ribbons or insignia on your uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which uniform? The first one, you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The very first one. We are at the first uniform, the very first that you were given by the emir of the 7th Mountain -- Muslim Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing. There were no insignia on that uniform. It was clean. It was just a soldier's uniform. Camouflage uniform. There were no insignia on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform made of what colours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Green, some brown, olive green. That is the kind of uniform it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you given any boots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, of this group of approximately ten foreign Mujahedin that were accommodated at Bilmiste barracks in April 1993, were you the only foreign Mujahedin who was provided with a military uniform?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I don't know whether others received one. I know I did. I don't know about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of clothing were the others wearing during the period they were accommodated with you at Bilmiste barracks in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: They were wearing uniforms. Someone main not be wearing the standard uniform or a costume like the Arab costume, but it was in camouflage material.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've told us about the two rooms that the foreign Mujahedin used in this building at Bilmiste barracks. Can you tell us, sir, about the other rooms in that building, who, if anyone, was accommodated there and what, if anything, was located in the other rooms of that building other than the two that you and the foreign Mujahedin were occupying?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The barracks was actually the school building. I think the secondary school. And the rooms were similar because they were classrooms. There was the command and the commander and all the others, the officers. They were all put up there. Then there was the communications centre, the canteen. Everything any unit has was accommodated in this school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, based upon your time there, can you tell us a little bit about the relationship between these eight to ten foreign Mujahedin and the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: It was nothing in particular. We would meet. They were at -- in the same building. Then we would meet in the canteen. Sometimes we would talk, but nothing special really, nothing in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than the group of eight to ten Arab Mujahedin that you were a member of and the soldiers of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, were there any other persons or groups billeted at Bilmiste barracks during the spring of 1993?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: What do you mean, Bosniaks or foreigners? What groups are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Any group, sir. You've told us about -- you've told us that at Bilmiste barracks there were soldiers of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, and there was a group of eight to ten Arab Mujahedin in the building, and my question was were there any other people or groups in that barracks building in the time period of spring 1993?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: There was a group of Turks who were put up in the gym, in the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Awad, anything about this group of Turks? How many? Who was in charge of them? What they were doing? Do you know any of these things about this group of Turks that were in the gym?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I know -- don't know. I just know that they were there. There was seven or eight of them. I didn't really go to look to see how many. There was a Kemal and a Jusuf as far as I was able to notice. I didn't have any real contact with them so that I don't have any more information about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown the document marked P01037. P01037.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to look at this document, Mr. Awad? Can you tell us anything about what's described in the first two paragraphs of this document?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: As far as I understand, they are addressing the command of the 3rd Corps, telling them that they have problems because foreign citizens have been detained by HVO people at check-points, and they're asking that such incidents should not be repeated in the future, and three names are mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know any of the three persons listed on this document?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I know that when people were released, when there was an exchange with the HVO, there was an Abu Kadir from Algeria, a Hadza Mohadji [phoen]. I don't really know his name. And someone from Tunisia. There was some from Kuwait and I think from Qatar, from the Emirates. There was even a Turk and a Pakistani in this exchange. So these are similar names to those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, approximately when this exchange that you've just mentioned took place and where?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: In 1993, in the summer. I don't know exactly which month, whether it was May or June. I can't remember the date. I don't know. But I know that it was in that period of time that there was an exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where did this exchange take place?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: In Zenica, in front of the hotel. I think it was called Internacional. Near the stadium in Zenica to be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who was exchanged at this encounter?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: There was an exchange. There was the commander of an HVO brigade, Zivko Totic, two other men, and they were exchanged for about 15 or 16 -- or between 13 and 15 men who were released on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who were these 13 to 15 men that were exchanged for Mr. Totic?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: One was a Bosnian. He was a driver. And the others were foreign volunteers who were arrested and detained at HVO check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did you personally have any involvement in organising or arranging this exchange?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Not a great deal. I was present when the exchange took place. I may have given some data when I was asked to do so, and I translated. I assisted in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who was responsible for organising or arranging this exchange?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Dr. Abu Haris coordinated with Mahmut Karalic the exchange, and he would talk to him in Arabic without any intermediary, that is without translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at -- at this point in time, sir, summer of 1993, what position did Mr. Karalic hold?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was known as emir. So he was an emir. What they meant by that I don't know, but that is how they called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And -- and when you say he was the emir or an emir, of what unit? What unit was he the emir of in the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Returning, sir, to this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if my learned friend could give a time frame for his question. The witness was answering questions about the exchange for Zivko Totic. I think this was in April 1993, and now the Prosecutor is continuing with questions when Mahmut Karalic was an emir. Could the Prosecutor please specify whether he is talking about the position of Efendija Karalic in April, or are we talking now about July 1993, to make things quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I understood the witness well, Madam Vidovic, I think he said it was around June when the exchange took place, and -- and that's the time frame that I understand Mr. Mundis to be talking about, the time in June and not April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps I can -- I can just clarify this with the witness briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, to the best of your recollection, when was this exchange that you've told us about that took place in Zenica where Colonel Totic was exchanged for 13 to 15 other persons?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I said a moment ago it may have been May or June. I wasn't sure. I didn't say June. I said maybe. Most probably it was in May, end of May. It could be. I can't remember exactly when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you told us a moment ago that Abu Haris and Mr. Karalic were involved in organising or arranging this exchange; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Abu Haris asked Mahmut Karalic that this exchange took place, that he should get in contact with the people for this exchange to take place. However, the exchange did not take place through Mahmut Karalic in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And -- and my question, sir, was the position that Mahmut Karalic held at the time Abu Haris was discussing this exchange with Mr. Karalic.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I'm repeating. I do not have a lot of information as to what was actually happening. I know that Amir Kubura was the commander, that Mahmut Karalic was called the emir. I've told you what I know. He was called an emir. Maybe he was still an emir. I know he was an emir at that time. Whether they changed it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, for the purposes of clarification, when you say Amir Kubura was the commander and Mr. Karalic was the emir, what unit are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I am referring to the 7th Muslim Brigade. I said that is how they called him. Now, why they called him that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's return, sir, briefly to the document that's in front of you. I'd like to draw your attention to the phrase in the first paragraph that says: "Arabs detained at Busovaca." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Awad, anything about this reference to Busovaca and particularly in the spring of 1993? What was in Busovaca? Who was in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't have a lot of information. I didn't stay there. I don't really know much about what was happening in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss the detention of these Arabs with any of the people who had been detained after their release?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I took the men to the hospital for them to be examined, to have a medical check-up. That is the men that were released on the occasion of the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who -- who had been holding them, and where were they being held?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The HVO captured them, and I think they were held at Kaonik, because representatives of UNPROFOR were at Kaonik. The detained don't know the names of those places, nor did I have contact with them to know exactly, but I heard the word "Kaonik." So maybe that was where they were held, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for purposes of clarity, sir, can you tell us what is Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: It's the name of a locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you -- can you -- can you be a little more precise? Where precisely is Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: On the road from Zenica towards Travnik, before one reaches Vitez. I think that is where it is. Maybe where the turning is for Busovaca and Kiseljak, and that place is called Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Awad?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution would ask that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 1126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 1126, thank you. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, I'd now like to turn your attention to the summer of 1993, the time period June and July 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If -- if you are going to go to the next period, can I just ask one little clarification? Sir, so far you have told us that there were about eight to ten Arab Mujahedin in the same building as the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, and then after you've told us -- you told us that you were doing nothing there. Then suddenly there is an exchange of people who have been captured. Can we assume from that that before this exchange there had been any fighting, or was there no fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the moment I got there these men did not take part in any fighting in that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the Arab people who were exchanged, particularly the three that are mentioned on Exhibit 1126, were they or were they not part of the eight to ten Mujahedin that were with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They couldn't be when they were detained. They were captured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, sir. All I'm asking you is the detained people were not people who were detained from your group, or did they come from another group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This group that I found there, eight to ten men who were put up at Bilmiste, I found them there roughly when this kidnapping took place. Now, whether these men belonged to this group or not I wasn't sure. I don't know, because I hadn't seen them before. So I can't say that they did or did not belong to this group. I just know that an exchange did take place, and there were many persons from different countries in that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what they were released, you took them to hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I took them to hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When they were discharged from hospital, did they come to your group or did they take their own route?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Bosnian went his way, the Turk went his way. Some of these men came. I think they went to Mehurici. Some left Bosnia-Herzegovina, so they weren't anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did any of those that were discharged from hospital come to your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Four or five. Four or five, I think, who -- whom I saw that they had stayed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And then your group increased from 8 to 10 to 18 to 15? Is that it? After these four or five came in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They stayed there briefly, and then they went on to Mehurici, because there wasn't sufficient accommodation for a large number of people, but only for people who needed to go to hospital or to do something, to talk to their families, to make phone calls or to buy some necessities. So this wasn't real accommodation for those Mujahedin, so that they had to go on. After they had finished the examinations, they left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Awad, I'd like to turn to your attention to the summer of 1993, the period June, July 1993. Where were -- where were you and your -- the group that you were in accommodated at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: We were still in that building at Bilmiste. That's where we stayed for a while. After that, these people, or a number of these people, left the building, the barracks, and they were no longer there in that will building, in those barracks in Bilmiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The people, foreign Mujahedin who left Bilmiste, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: We went to Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately when and what time period did this group go, relocate from Bilmiste to Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I cannot be certain, but after these events, the exchange and after what happened, maybe 10 or 15 days later these people left and went to Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when this group of people went to Mehurici, did you go with them, or did you stay at Bilmiste, or did you go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: No, no. I stayed at Bilmiste for a while. I was still there at Bilmiste still in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did anyone else from the group of foreign Mujahedin that had been there with you in April remain in Bilmiste in June, July 1993?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: There was just Abu Mali, myself. I think Ejub and another person who were preparing food for the wounded and that they were taking to the hospital. I don't think that there was anyone else. I think there was one person from Egypt, Abu Bula, something like that. He was there as well, I think, but the rest had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what role or function was Abu Mali holding or occupying? What position did he have in June, July 1993?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: He was in charge of the people who were billeted at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What language or languages did Abu Mali speak at that time?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: He spoke Arabic and also he had learned or picked up some Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Awad, did there come a time when you were no longer accommodated at Bilmiste barracks?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific so that I know how to answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, sir, in April of 1993 that you were accommodated in Bilmiste barracks. For how long did you remain primarily accommodated at Bilmiste barracks?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: About two months or three months. I said that. It was a short period. It didn't last that long, for months or years. It was just a brief period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Right. And my question, sir, is after this brief two- to three-month period, where were you staying or where were you accommodated?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: After that we moved to the Podbrezje area, the building that we were given as our command and for our accommodation, because the unit will be founded later, because the unit was established in August and then we moved to that building, and we didn't have any other accommodation in place. We were only in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall, sir, the name of this building in Podbrezje that you've just been talking about?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: It belonged to the Vatrostalna company. So the build being itself was also called Vatrostalna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Awad, I'd like to turn your attention to the summer of 1993, the period specifically June and July 1993. Were you aware of any combat operations or military operations in that time period in the area where you were located?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Except for what happened in Zenica, there were no activities in the Zenica area where I was accommodated. When the conflict broke out between the Bosnia and Herzegovina army and the HVO, then the Vatrostalna building belonged earlier to the HVO Brigade command. I don't know which brigade. And it was liberated then. They left that building. After that I didn't hear that there was any fighting or battles in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go to the slightly wider geographic area. Do you know, sir, or were you involved in any military operations or combat operations in the Bila valley in June, July 1993?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: On one occasion Wahiuddeen visited Zenica. He was the Mujahedin emir. He came from Mehurici to visit Zenica, and on the way back to Mehurici I expressed a wish to go and see where the people were accommodated, to see where the Mujahedin lived, and I went with him over the hill via Sarici, the village of Sarici, and then we went to some hill, and then you reach the Jezerci and then you go down to Mehurici. On that occasion -- that was actually the first time that I came to that area, and I was in the camp there. We stayed there for a short time, and then he left for Guca Gora. And I went with him, and I think that Abu Mali was with us as well. We got to Guca Gora. We reached a monastery, and that's where we found some local commander. I don't know. And there were two other people with him. And Wahiuddeen knew them from before, and he spoke with them, and what I understood was that that was when Guca Gora was liberated. And then after that -- or actually the next day, the Mujahedin were supposed to attack an area across from Guca Gora. I think it was called Radojcici or something. Please don't hold me to the exact word. And since I was new and didn't have any military experience, that morning I was there -- or Abu Haris actually charged me with dealing with the wounded, and that was near the Guca Gora cemetery. That's the only time that I took part in those operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me go back and ask you some follow-on questions from that answer that you've just given us. On this occasion when you went with Wahiuddeen by way of Sarici to Mehurici, was that the first time you'd been in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I said that it was the first time that I was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about what you saw in Mehurici, this location that you went to with Wahiuddeen?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: We came to the camp, as they called it, and there were two houses there, one opposite from the other, and there was a sort of clearing, clear area, in the middle. There was one path through a small wood, and there was another house there. So that was more or less the camp. I saw two or three people there at that time who happened to be there, visible. I saw two or three people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who was in charge of this camp at that time when you were there in June or July 1993?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I don't know. I was there for the first time. I didn't know the people. It was the first time for me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know or were you told approximately how many people, how many Mujahedin, foreign Mujahedin, were accommodated at that camp in the summer of 1993?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I really don't know. I didn't really think about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: You also told us a few moments ago that the foreign Mujahedin were supposed to be involved in combat in the area of Radojcici.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember anything about what they were supposed to do or how many foreign fighters were supposed to be involved in that operation concerning Radojcici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. At no point did the witness mention any assignment or task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll certainly seek to clarify that, but my recollection is that he did say that they were supposed to be involved in an operation in Radojcici, but I'll reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you please do, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is correct what the Prosecutor said, to take part in an operation or an action, but to have an assignment or a task is something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There you go, Mr. Mundis. There's the distinction between what you are asserting and what the Defence counsel's objecting against.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- let me ask you this, Mr. Awad: Do you recall what you were told about Radojcici on this occasion when you were there with Wahiuddeen?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I know that the HVO forces were there on some hill up there, and the Mujahedin were supposed to attack that area. They set off to attack that area. I heard also that some other people were supposed to go with them, but, however, that morning only those Mujahedin were attacking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us or do you know, sir, approximately how many Mujahedin were involved in this attack on Radojcici against the HVO forces?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I think that there were perhaps 60 people, maybe a bit more. I didn't really pay attention because I wasn't there during the preparation, so I don't know the exact number. I think that there were two groups, so it could have been 40 to 60 people. It's possible. I mean, that's how it usually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And do you know where these groups had come from or where they had been accommodated?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I would like to just note this: When I gave my statement, I was speculating, guessing. So I cannot really be more specific when I don't know, and I don't know the terrain. I don't know exactly where they had come from. I know that the assembly point was at the monastery in Guca Gora and that they were supposed to go off and attack from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How -- how do you know, sir, that they were supposed to go and attack Radojcici from this assembly point at Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I had heard that the assembly point was at Guca Gora, and that morning I was present there, but I wasn't present when they set off for the battle because I was there where the wounded were, but I understood that this was the assembly point and that they would leave for the field from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Awad, who was in charge of this attack and Radojcici which these two groups of Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The attack was executed with -- in two groups in two axes. One group was led by Mutas [phoen], the late Ahmed Ali, and the other group was led by Hasan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please repeat, sir, the last name of this person Hasan?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Not Hasan but Husa Mudin [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And did you actually see either of these groups assembly at Guca Gora on that day?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I saw them in Guca Gora. I saw them in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, if you know, about the composition of these groups in terms of the fighters that you saw? Where were they from?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Foreigners, and there were also a few Bosnians there, yes. It was mixed. Both Bosnians and Arabs were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How do you know that there were also Bosnians there?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: They're Bosnians. I saw people who were Arabs and people who were Bosnians. I know that they were Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How do you know that, Mr. Awad?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Well, they speak the Bosnian language. So when they communicate amongst themselves, they speak Bosnian. They could have been Siptars also who had learned to speak Bosnian. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I'm -- I'm about to turn to a completely new subject, and this might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, let's just find out. Mr. Awad, now that you're speaking Bosnian to us today, can we assume that you are Bosnian? I'm just trying to say to you, Mr. Awad, do you conclude the nationality of people simply from the language they speak? And if that is so, can I then say you are Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, maybe -- up until maybe six months ago you could have said that I was a Bosnian. I'm no longer a Bosnian because my citizenship has been revoked. But they looked different. Their features were different. They're not the same people. Arabs have a known physiology. Well, maybe my -- my skin tone is a little different, but you can tell that I'm an Arab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. That's why Mr. Prosecutor is asking you these questions as to how did you tell, because he assumes that you did not look at their citizenship cards. Now, we know that you may not be a Bosnian because your citizenship has been taken away. But you didn't see the ID documents of these people. When you see people standing in a group there, how did you determine that these were Bosnians, those were Croats, and -- if there is anything over and above the language that you did observe? If there is nothing, "Mr. Prosecutor, that's all I observed," that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I noticed -- I didn't ask anyone for their identification or ask them to introduce themselves and say who their father was, where they were born. I didn't take their particulars, but you could conclude, and it's my assumption, that they were Bosnians on the basis of the fact that they were speaking Bosnians -- Bosnian. I understand their language. Foreigners can never speak Bosnian so fluently no matter how well they learn it. You could always hear a difference in speech, in the manner of expression, and so on. So on the basis of that I was able to conclude that they were Bosnians. I didn't have any other arguments or details, and I didn't ask them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this might be an appropriate time for -- for the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There's a question before we take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we have just a couple of minutes before we can take the break, I would like to take this opportunity to then raise a small issue that I felt could be taken up during the Prosecutor's examination-in-chief, and the issue I am thinking about is the reasons why you came to Bosnia in the first place. I wonder if you could explain to us why you took off from Syria, I suppose, Bosnia, and if you could tell us who organised the trip and if any motivation was given to you by the people who assisted you to go to Bosnia. I think you told us you came to Belgrade and then you went off to Zagreb and only then did you come to Bosnia, but why did you take off from the Middle East to -- to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I left Syria with the intention of studying medicine in the former Yugoslavia, and this is why I came to the former Yugoslavia. Since the main airport was in Belgrade, we first landed in Belgrade. Then we took the train from Belgrade to Zagreb where I spent three years. And first I learned the language, Croato-Serbian. Then I enrolled at the medical faculty where I spent two years studying, and then I transferred to another town, to Rijeka - this is another town in Croatia - to continue my studies, Rijeka. And then I was seven years in Rijeka. In 1992, when the aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina occurred and when Bosnians -- Bosniaks were expelled and waves of refugees arrived in Croatia, some of them also came to Rijeka where I was living and staying, and together with the Islamic community and Merhamet and other organisations I started to work with them in order to help those people. When I saw and heard from them what had happened to them, what horrors and massacres they went through, I decided as a Muslim, as a young man -- I had a feeling that it was my duty as a Muslim by faith to help these Muslims, and this is why I came to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Nobody organised me. Nobody paid for my trip. Yes, I used a humanitarian organisation through which I came to Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I can say that I came at their expense, but they didn't pay me for it. But my pure intention as a man of faith, as a Muslim, was to help the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's why I came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you involved in the organisation of more people from the Middle East to come to the former Yugoslavia to assist in the humanitarian tasks in Bosnia when the war had started? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand. I didn't have any contacts, but when the aggression against Bosnia and Herzegovina started, different Islamic humanitarian organisations arrived, and they were mostly located in Zagreb, and they asked students -- they were looking for students who could work with them, who understood the language of the region, who could help them and make their work easier, so I offered to volunteer. I offered to help these people, and I voluntarily went to help these people. I volunteered with these humanitarian organisations. Otherwise, I would not have had any contact with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Awad. We will take a short break and come back at 11.00. We will carry on at 11.00, Mr. Awad. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, earlier this morning you mentioned the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment, and I'd knew like to ask you some -- some more detailed questions about that. Do you know, sir, or can you tell us anything about how the decision was made to form the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, if you could just pause. I don't seem to be getting --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The microphone was not switched on. Could the witness repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you, please, Mr. Awad, again repeat your answer so that those of us who don't speak Bosnian can understand what you're saying, please.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: We made a request that a unit be formed that would be called the literal translation from the Arabic, and I will tell you, it is called Kasib su El Mujahedin [phoen], which means the El Mujahedin Unit in Bosnian. How this decision was made to form this unit I don't know because I wasn't in the General Staff, but I know that on the basis of that request that such a unit was formed. Now, how it was given this name, I don't know. Our request was that this unit be called the El Mujahedin Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you some follow-up questions, sir. When you say "we made the request," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I am referring to a group of men whose emir was Dr. Abu Haris. That is this group which decided to form the unit, the El Mujahedin Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more about this request? What form did it take? What language was it in, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And to whom was it addressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The request was written in Arabic. I personally translated it into Bosnian, and I personally took it to the command of the 3rd Corps and handed it in to the protocol section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who wrote the request in Arabic, if you know?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure was it Wahuiddeen or Molda [phoen]. I got the text in Arabic, and I translated it into Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I don't believe, sir, the interpreter heard you with respect to the second name. Do you recall the name or names of the people that you think drafted the document in Arabic?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The document was written, I think, Wahiuddeen or Muadep [phoen], one of the two. I'm not quite sure. I received it in Arabic and translated it into Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, I believe the interpreter may have had a hard time. Did you say Muazed [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: No. Muatez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, you think the Arabic was drafted by either Wahuiddeen or Muatez?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Either Wahuiddeen or Muatez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the approximate time period or date that you delivered this Bosnian language version of the request to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: It could have been the end of June or the month of July. In any event, I remember after I returned from the area of Guca Gora that this happened, but I can't be quite sure when this was. I didn't pay attention to dates, months, and so on, but it was when I came back from Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for the record, 3rd Corps of what army?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which army?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, you told us you took it to the protocol department or office. Where was that located?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: In the building of the command of the 3rd Corps. On the ground floor. When you walk in, to the left. This is where there was a room for the protocol, and that is where you would hand in requests or letters or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you -- can you tell us where this building was physically located?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: In Zenica. Across the road from the ironworks headquarters, near the gate, I think. Today this building is used for the customs administration office in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On the day, Mr. Awad, that you took this request to the protocol office, had you ever been in that building before or was that the first time you ever went there?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: No. That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And perhaps we'll get to this a little bit later in your testimony, but at this point I would just ask you, sir, if that was the first and only time you were ever in that building or if you ever went into that brigade on subsequent occasions.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: When that request was handed in was the only time I went there. After the El Mujahedin Detachment was formed, I went to that building on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And on the day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I am still seeking to understand why was the request made in the first place to the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll get to that, Your Honour, but if I can just -- one or two more questions on this line and we'll get to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, on the day that you went there, did you -- to take this request, did you go by yourself or were you accompanied by anyone?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to that issue. Why -- if you know, why did the leadership of the Arab Mujahedin want this detachment to be created?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: In my view there are two main reasons. With the Arab Mujahedin there was a group of Bosniaks who had left their units around joined the Arabs, and they fought with them. They were fighters, combatants. But their units considered them to be deserters. They sent the military police to arrest them and so on. And their families couldn't realise their rights in terms of medical care and such similar things, so they had to have some kind of regular status. They didn't wish to go back to their original units. They wanted to stay with the Arabs, with the Mujahedin. And the second reason was that the battles that were ongoing and whatever the Mujahedin were doing should be legal, because there were various stories. Various things were happening. So we wanted this group of people to be distinguished from the free-fighters, so to speak, and others. So those are the two main reasons. First, to protect the Bosniaks so that they should no longer be treated as deserters. They were army members, but their units considered them to be deserters. And the second reason was for this group of people who would fight together with these Bosniaks to be considered legal fighters of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn to the subject of the request, that is the form of the request. Do you remember -- do you recall what the request actually said?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I can't remember verbatim, but it was roughly of the following content: "We are addressing you," that is the command of the 3rd Corps, "to approve the formation of the unit El Mujahedin," and then a description was given of the -- of how this unit would be organised, who the commander would be. It was stated that the commander of the unit is Dr. Abu Haris, who would be accommodated at Mehurici, and their representative in Zenica would be Abu Mali. Then also the military commander of that unit would be -- or, rather, the person responsible for military matters would be Wahiuddeen, and his representative in Zenica would be Muatez. His real name is El Muatez Elbul [phoen]. So don't -- so as not to confuse you, we call him just Muatez for short. This request also stated that the unit would have its emblem, which would appear as follows: Two rifles in this form, in the middle an open book, and above and below in Arabic and in Bosnian on top -- it doesn't matter where -- which would be -- "Sidiem el El Jihad" [phoen] in Arabic, and in Bosnian "Our road is jihad."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let the record show that when the witness said, "two against in this form," he crossed his fingers in an X form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not a cross. It's like a cross, but it's not a cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I said you crossed your fingers in the form of an X.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: X.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. Not -- not in the form of a Christian cross. And I'm aware of that, Mr. Awad. I will never say that to you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I heard in translation the word "cross," and that is why I reacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And just crossed in the form of an X. X, the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, do we have a copy of the request?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, let me -- let me ask you, do you recall whether in addition to the request that -- the parts that you told us, was any other information provided?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I think that this request contained only these information that I mentioned, as far as I can recollect. Maybe there were some other points, but these were the main points contained in the request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were any other documents forwarded to the 3rd Corps along with this request?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I can't be specific. There may have been a list of names. I can't remember, but I know that the request was submitted, but for other documents I can't say for sure. I don't remember for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate or give a specific number of this group that decided that they must forward this request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The group consisted of between 60 and 70 men, and the first list that was filed had a number of a hundred or maybe a hundred and one names, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So there was a list that was submitted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe not at the same time when the gentleman was asking me about the time of the request, but subsequently other documents were submitted. But as far as I can remember, this first list contained a hundred or a hundred and one names. And this document is in the possession of the court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I saw this document when I testified in another case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Awad. That's very helpful. Yes, Mr. Mundis, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This list that you've mentioned with a hundred or a hundred and one names on it, do you know, sir, if all of those names were names of foreigners or was it a mixture of Bosnian names and foreign names?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, I think they were foreign names. As far as I can remember. I can't be quite certain. There may have been a couple of Bosnian names, but the majority were certainly foreign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Awad, what happened with respect to the formation of the detachment after this written request was delivered by you to the headquarters of the 3rd Corps in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: On the 13th of August, 1993, an order was issued to form a military unit, that is the El Mujahedin Detachment, and that is when it was formed. Officially there was a kind of celebration of the foundation of that unit. On the 13th of August, 1993, the order arrived that the El Mujahedin Detachment be formed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Awad, when you say the order arrived, can you tell us from where it arrived?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I think it came through the 3rd Corps. Now, whether it was through the 3rd Corps or the Operative Group Bosanska Krajina -- I'm not quite sure who gave us this document, but in any event, it came from the General Staff of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mundis, I know we've just come back from a break, but today we are supposed to break a little early to accommodate the witness. How much longer are you going to be? We have gone past the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yeah. I think this would actually -- this was about where I was planning on stopping. This would be a convenient place to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good. Thank you very much, Mr. Mundis. If that is a time, we will then take a break and come back at half past 1.00. We will come back at half past 1.00, so will give you time. Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, right before the lunch break we were talking about the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment, and you mentioned a gathering that occurred. Can you tell us, sir, if you recall approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: What gathering?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The gathering when the El Mujahedin Detachment was formally formed. The formation ceremony.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: After we received the order on the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment, in the Mehurici camp a formal sort of ceremony was organised to mark the proclamation, and present there were people from the command of the BH army, that is, of the command of the 3rd Corps, the command of the Operative Group Bosanska Krajina, and some other people, public figures from civilian life in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, if you recall approximately the date of this ceremony in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. It was in August, but what day I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In which -- which year?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you -- can you perhaps narrow it down in terms of reference to the order that you mentioned officially forming the detachment?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: No, I can't remember. I know that it took place in August, but I don't know exactly on what day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you just mentioned the positions of a number of people who attended. Can you fill in or provide us with the names of some of these more prominent individuals who attended this formation ceremony in Mehurici in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Present at the ceremony were the late General Mehmed Alagic, General Sakib Mahmuljin, the head of Travnik municipality. I think his name was Muhamed Dzuric. Also the Muftija of Travnik, Nusret Abdibegovic. Also present were other figures, other persons. Mahmudin [phoen], Dr. Abu Haris, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you present?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir -- you've again mentioned some names. Can you tell us, if you -- if you know or if you remember, what position did the late General Alagic hold in August 1993 when he attended this formation ceremony?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I think he was still commander of the Operative Group. I think he was commander of the Bosanska Krajina Operative Group. I think he was still commander at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At that time, August 1993, do you know what position Sakib Mahmuljin held?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I don't know. He was not chief of staff or corps commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say he was not chief of staff or corps commander, which corps and army are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I'm referring to the 3rd Corps, because later he became chief of staff when the corps commander was the late Mehmed Alagic. He was corps commander. And Sakib Mahmuljin became chief of staff of that corps. Later the 7th Corps was formed, and there was a separation between these two corps, the 3rd and the 7th. Mehmed Alagic became commander of the 7th Corps, and Sakib Mahmuljin commander of the 3rd. That is why I said that he wasn't chief of staff or corps commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, approximately when this -- the 7th Corps was formed and Sakib Mahmuljin became 3rd Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Maybe at the end of 1993 or the beginning of 1994, but certainly not in August. After that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You have mentioned a few of the members of the detachment who were present. I believe you said Dr. Haris. Do you recall how many members of the detachment attended this ceremony in Mehurici in August 1993?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Not more than 60 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On this occasion, sir, were you serving or working as interpreter?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was anyone else interpreting at this formation ceremony or were you the only interpreter present on that day?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: When Dr. Abu Haris addressed those present, Abdul Melik interpreted for Dr. Abu Haris. I was sitting on a bench between General Mehmed Alagic and General Sakib Mahmuljin, who is now a general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we would like to show the witness a videotape which has been marked P06146, P06146, and I would ask the assistance of the audiovisual booth in showing that or assisting us in showing that video. This -- this video runs approximately two minutes and ten seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May the audiovisual booth please help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could play that again. We do have a version that has a synchronised transcript associated with it, so if we can perhaps start the video again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. President, is the witness the person who is standing next to the speaker?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I was intending on doing is playing the full clip, and then we'll go back and stop and have the witness identify certain individuals that he might be in a position to identify, but I would prefer to show him the entire thing and then we'll go back and play it and stop and pause and have him identify people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If I can just perhaps explain. My understanding from my case manager is that if we show it full screen we lose the transcript, so what we'll now do is I will propose playing the video in the full screen mode without the audio and ask the witness if he can identify any of the persons depicted, if that's an acceptable way to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you -- Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was asking, actually, if the Prosecutor has a section on this footage of the speech of the Arabs. Obviously you can see a person with a beard in the footage, and from what the witness said before, Abdul Melik was translating. The witness speaks Arabic, and it would be very useful if in this part of the footage that the Prosecutor showed we could listen to the original Arabic that the witness could then confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you understand what Madam Vidovic is asking of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I do indeed, and I'm not sure if we have the full clip with us here on the laptop. I -- I would propose that perhaps the first thing we do is have the witness identify people for the benefit of the record. We'll then see if we have the clip that actually contains or that -- that the Arabic portion is audible, and then perhaps we can proceed as Mrs. Vidovic indicates.
