I would be happy to do that, assuming that we have the proper clip that has the Arabic language being audible for long enough to actually make any sense out of what's -- what's contained and the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Madam Vidovic, do you look forward to the witness interpreting from the Arabic for us, or how do you propose that we understand the Arabic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thought that the witness could in any case listen to the version in Arabic and then we would also all listen to this part that the Prosecutor chose, and then the witness who speaks both languages would be in the position to see if the interpretation actually corresponds to what the man is saying. Otherwise, all we're hearing is the interpretation of the Bosnian person without hearing the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And perhaps if we can't get this sorted at this moment, maybe we can return to that tomorrow morning having had the chance to fully review the tapes. I'm not sure Ms. Imamovic will be able to hear anything without -- without broadcasting it to all of us. So let me -- let me start by saying this:

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did you -- I know the image was very small on the computer. Did you recognise what was shown in that videotape?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, isn't it better to play the video now without a transcript so that he can begin to see, and he can tell us this is so-and-so, that is so-and-so? We can also see the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We're going to play the tape again, Mr. Awad, in the full-screen mode without the sound, and I would ask you if you recognise anyone on the tape to simply say, "Stop," as soon as you see a person or persons that you recognise, and we will pause the tape, and I will then ask you to identify the person or persons that you see on the tape. That clear? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. We have Midhat Puric here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which person is Mr. Puric? Can you describe perhaps what he looks like and what he's wearing?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The footage is not all that clear. You cannot really see it distinctly that Hadzija was a member of the army. He was not part of the El Mujahedin Unit. He's wearing a uniform. I don't see the colour of his beret. I don't see if it's blue or black because the footage is grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us approximately where on the screen you see Mr. Puric?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Directly -- it's the first person we can see. If we look from the left side, you can see that it's the first person whose face you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That the person with something like spectacles or dark glasses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no, no. The person with the dark glasses I cannot see. I don't see anything all the way to the left, but this first person at that we see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, are we not able to write on the screens like we do back home?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we're not able to do that. I will indicate for the record that this is at 10 seconds on this clip as indicated at the bottom of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us -- can you tell us, Mr. Awad, Mr. Puric, where are his hands in this picture?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Like this in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let the record show that the witness demonstrates with his hands that the person he's referring to is the person whose fingers are spread out with the outside of the hand showing on the table. He has described this person as wearing a beret. He can't say the beret's blue or black. And the person is wearing a uniform, an army uniform. That seems to be the only visible person dressed like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you say Mr. Puric was in the army, do you know what army he was in and perhaps what unit of that army he was?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: He's a member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think that he was in some brigade, maybe the 314th or -- I don't know exactly which one, but he's a member of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll continue now, sir, with the videotape and, again, simply say, "Stop," as soon as you see any person or persons that you recognise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'll go back to the ten second part of the tape.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: This is that same person. It's the same person that was sitting like this. It's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, for the record, his name?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: He is Hadzija Midhat Puric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for the record, we're now at 18 seconds on this video clip. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. On my right side -- or on the right-hand side we see the late General Mehmed Alagic. Next to him is Sakib Mahmuljin, sitting next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the record, we're at 23 seconds on the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, can you perhaps give further identification in terms of the colour of these two individuals' hair? Which is which?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The one on the right is something that is black and white. It's black and white. And the other person is pure black. So the late Alagic has some black in his hair, and General Mahmuljin has all black hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could continue, please, with the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. In this frame the very first person on the screen is Dr. Abu Haris, and behind him is the interpreter Abdul.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the other name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you -- could you please repeat the name of the interpreter for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Abdul Melik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again for the record, we're at 28 seconds on this tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a clarification question, Mr. Awad. When you say the first person, are you referring to someone who's holding an automatic weapon, or are you referring to someone else?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: No, no. The first in relation to me. The first one on the screen is Abu Haris, and then from my point of view is then Abdul Melik standing next to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, do you mean that the nearest person to the viewer of the picture as we look at the picture, that person who is closest to the camera. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This would be the bearded person who doesn't have any headgear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope I have not done anything wrong, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In we could please --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please continue with the videotape then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Awad, did you --

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The -- the images are not sharp enough. I cannot recognise anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this, though, sir, before we -- we leave this tape: Did you see yourself anywhere depicted on the videotape? Did you recognise yourself anywhere on the tape?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I did, but by the time I said stop it had already passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we go back there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's go back to -- it's [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Indiscernible]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's go back to the beginning of the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have time and you have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please stop there. Are you able to read what's written there, Mr. Awad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The image is not sharp. It's not in focus. Maybe in a different place I could see it better, I could read it. I mean, I know what it says, but I want to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yeah, we would like you to read it for us. We'll wait and see if it ever comes in a clearer form than that. I don't remember seeing it any clearer, but we may carry on with -- with the tape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stop. [Interpretation] This is me on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And we're -- for the benefit of the record, we're at 21 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Awad, when you say, "This is me on the left-hand side," can you describe --

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: There's something else. Wahiuddeen Ali is on the extreme right of this frame. On my left side the person with the paper, that's me. And then on the extreme left side is the -- is Wahid Mehmed Sumali [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's -- let's -- let's take them one at a time, Mr. Awad. The person you've identified as yourself you said has some papers in his hand. Is that person sitting or standing?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Sitting. Sitting. Just like I'm sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, the person you've described as Wahiuddeen, where is he on this image?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: All the way to the right. On the screen it's right at the end on the right-hand side, and he's holding his hands like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I'd like the record to reflect that when the witness said "like this," he again held his hands together, clasped his fingers together. And again we're at 21 seconds on the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, can you tell us what, if anything, Mr. Wahiuddeen has on his head?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: He's wearing a cap, a cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can then play the tape to see if the witness is able to read what's contained on the banner.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Slowly, please. Okay, stop. Stop. What is says is: "La elaha, elaha [phoen]." "There is no other God than Allah and no other emissary than Mohamed." So Mohamed is the messenger of Allah. And then in Bosnian underneath that it says "Brig," and you don't see the whole word. And then the other word is "Jihad." So it should "Brigada Jihad," "Brigade Jihad."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again for the record, this is at 24 seconds on this videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. While we're at this piece here, is the Jihad Brigade synonymous with --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's the precise -- precisely where I'm going, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, can you explain to us, if you know, why this banner says in Bosnian "Brigada Jihad"?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: From what I understood, these people, Bosniaks who are bearing this banner, they were hoping that the military units that would be formed would be called Brigada Jihad. I concluded that on the basis of the speech by the interpreter earlier, because he finally says -- he says that finally Al Jihad or Jihad Unit has been formed. So that is probably what they were thinking, that that would be what the unit would be called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In fact, sir, what was the name of the unit that was formed?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The unit that was formed then was given the name the El Mujahedin Detachment. I explained before the break that when the request was submitted, I wrote that the El Mujahedin Unit should be formed. I didn't pick the name. Somebody thought it would be a battalion or a brigade. As far as I was concerned, it would be a unit. Now, why was it decided to have the El Mujahedin Detachment as the name and not a brigade or jihad is something that I actually don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, of any unit -- are you familiar with any unit that had the official name Brigada Jihad?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I didn't hear of anything like that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Awad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question. Witness, during the ceremony there was no mention that such a different name would be given to the unit, that is the El Mujahedin Unit, rather than Brigada Jihad? Was that mentioned at all at the ceremony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat the question? I didn't quite hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the ceremony, was any reference made to the fact that this unit would not be called Brigada Jihad but that it would be called the El Mujahedin Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember exactly how the speech went, how this was expressed. If it was in Arabic, then he probably said what I said earlier. The witness speaks Arabic. And this can have many meanings. Katiba [phoen] can mean battalion, can be a bigger or a larger unit. It can even be a brigade. Katiba. So it's a gathering, a group, a larger number of people who are fighting for something. They can be named Katiba. So if in Arabic this was used, Katiba El Mujahedin, the official name in Bosnia would be Odred El Mujahedin, El Mujahedin Detachment. These Bosniaks and even a lot of other people called this unit El Jihad until the end of the war. They were mixing it up. People didn't know the correct term. We can even request farther. Journalists and plenty of people to this day refer to the El Mujahid Detachment, but that was not the name of the unit. The name of the unit was El Mujahedin Detachment. Sometimes they would say member of the El Mujahid Detachment. So even if it was mentioned, it was not so -- it was not possible to explain it so well in the ceremony, and you could interpret the words of the speaker in different ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would tender P06146 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P06146 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 1127, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order to save time, I would suggest perhaps that immediately upon the completion of today's session that the Defence meet with us and we'll try to identify a portion of this tape that might have some Arabic audio bits audible to proceed along the lines as Mrs. Vidovic has suggested. I'm afraid it might eat up valuable court time for us to try to do that now, but we can certainly revisit the issue in the morning with the witness and perhaps after we've all had a chance to try to find a proper clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That -- is that okay with you, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The parties may do that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Awad, let me ask you, sir, upon the formation of the El Mujahedin Detachment, were you a member of that unit?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For how long did you remain a member of the El Mujahedin Detachment following the formation of that unit?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: From the time the decision was made to form the unit, when it was officially formed, until the moment when the unit was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when, to the best of your recollection, was the unit disbanded?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: In December 1995, after the signing of the Dayton agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We'll certainly return to that topic of the disbandment of the unit later, but my question now, sir, is what was your role or what was your capacity, what -- in what way did you function as a member of the El Mujahedin Detachment from August 1993 through December 1995?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I worked as an interpreter. In the beginning until the end I was the translator or interpreter in that unit. On paper, formally, it says that I was the deputy -- assistant commander for security, assistant commander for security. But never actually carried out those duties, nor do I know how to carry them out. So that's why I say that from the beginning until the end I was the interpreter or translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, for whom did you interpret or translate?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Mostly for the commander of the El Mujahedin Detachment. Sometimes also for Mutaza [phoen], this is, for the military commander, El Mutaza.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, Mr. Awad, that you interpreted for the commander, what person are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I have in mind the commander of the detachment. First it was Dr. Abu Haris, then Abu Mali. The -- but he is still alive. Dr. Abu Haris, and Abu Melik [as interpreted] as the commanders. For a while for Wahiuddeen before he was killed, but he was not the commander. He was just responsible for military matters, and I attended a meeting with him when I interpreted for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps there was a bit of confusion, at least in the English it sounded as though you said the commander of the unit was Abu Melik.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Abu El Mahali.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, sir, in what type of setting your services as an interpreter or translator would be required?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I said that people didn't know the Bosnian language, so they needed somebody to interpret, to explain when something was being said, whether it was a meeting with someone or one of the soldiers. Members of the detachment wanted to address the commander. Somebody needed to explain to the commander what it was. So it was my duty to interpret, to pass on, to convey whatever was being said during those contacts or meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you just -- we'll go into this in much greater detail in a few moments, but can you just tell us what these meetings were that you've referred to, what types of meetings?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: There were different types of meetings. When the commander of the unit needed something or when he wanted to talk to the corps commander or to the commander of the Operative Group, then I would interpret. And this is a kind of meeting. I even interpreted at meetings when, for instance, we went to the factory Novi Travnik to purchase weapons. Again I was there as an interpreter. These are the meetings I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you make reference to meetings with the corps commander, what corps are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: When I talk about the corps, I am referring to the 3rd Corps. When I say "the army," I mean the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We were not in the HVO or any other body -- any other army, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about the operation group? You said also meetings with the commander of the Operational Group. What Operational Group or groups were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I am referring to the Operational Group, for instance, that was called the Bosanska Krajina. A meeting was held before Wahiuddeen was killed in Dubac, and there was a meeting with unit commanders, the commanders of the units who took part in the combat operations around Vitez and this terrain. Wahiuddeen was called to the meeting, and I was there with him, and I interpreted those talks that they had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, to my learned friend and to you for interfering, but I think it is important to set a time frame for the questions and answers of the witness as precisely as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yeah. That's precisely what I was about to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, this meeting that you've referred to concerning combat in the area around Vitez, what time period are you referring to? When was that?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: End of August -- no, end September. In September 1993 to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you -- can you tell us, sir, where this meeting occurred?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I said -- the place is called Lupac. It's a locality close to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was at Lupac? Why did you go there to have this meeting?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I think that a forward command post was there of the Operational Group, and that is where these meetings were held with the commander of the Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And now, sir, you've made reference to meetings in the plural. How many such meetings do you recall in September 1993 at this forward command post in Lupac?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I said a moment ago I attended one meeting with Wahiuddeen at that location. When I said meetings were being held, I meant that meetings were held at the forward command post where it is normal for the commander to hold meetings with his other commanders. I personally attended only one such meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you recall, sir, who was present from the Bosanska Krajina operation group?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The late General Mehmed Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, the topic or topics of discussion at this meeting in September 1993 in Lupac between Wahiuddeen and the late General Alagic?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: There wasn't a lot of talk. Wahiuddeen just presented the facts that people were on the ground and that these combat operations needed to be continued. As far as I understood, there had already been an attack and that it should be continued. General Alagic, the late General, ordered his commanders to continue the battles that they had to fight. All of them as one were complaining, "We can't go on. We don't have sufficient forces. We look ammunition," and so on. There were comments of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir -- when you say he ordered his commanders, do you recall what commanders were present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I think the commander of the 325th Brigade was present. I don't know whether there was anyone from the 17th Krajina Brigade. I can't remember exactly who was present. But anyway, the units that were taking part in those operations. So their commanders or their representatives were present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, whether the late General Alagic gave any specific taskings to Wahiuddeen and the El Mujahedin Detachment at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: No. There was nothing specific. It was just stated that the operation should be continued, that the combat must be continued together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, following this meeting in Lupac in September 1993, did in fact the combat continue in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: We returned, Wahiuddeen and myself, to Kruscica where the El Mujahedin Unit was stationed, and then they tried to carry out an attack against a position called Crveno Brdo, I think, but we had many wounded, high losses, and we couldn't reach that spot where the men were assigned to go, that is, to continue the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mention -- you mention, Mr. Awad, operations in the area of Kruscica. Do you know whose idea it was to undertake operations in Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I don't know with certainty because this was the first time for me to go out into the area, because I spent more of my time in the barracks. So I was not aware of the plans or what had been agreed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Before turning, sir, to 1994, I'd like to ask you some more general questions that are applicable throughout the entire period you were with the detachment from August 1993 through December 1995. So I'm talking about that whole period that you were in the detachment. Can you tell us, Mr. Awad, who set the combat priorities for the El Mujahedin Detachment in terms of where the unit was to go, what areas were to be attacked, what areas were to be defended, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: It is logical that the priorities would be set by the commanders, either of the corps or the operations group. That is the persons who had several units under their command, because the El Mujahedin Detachment as a small unit cannot determine where others would attack nor where they themselves would attack. So it is only logical and normal for the people who are in charge of several brigades or several units to plan and to determine the priorities where defences should be reinforced, where an attack should be launched, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, how were these priorities communicated to the leadership of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: In the following way: When an operation had to be carried out or an attack, we would be called in by the command of the operations group. This was in 1993. Later on all these arrangements were made at the level of the corps command. And occasionally at the level of the operations group, but mostly at the level of the corps command. So we would be called to go to the corps command for a talk, and then we would be informed that the unit should prepare for a particular attack and that we should take part together with those units. We would be attached to another unit as we were small in number at first, at the beginning. So we [as interpreted] would give us people who were aware of the terrain, who would show us the terrain. Our people would do reconnaissance, and after this reconnaissance the attack would be carried out along the axis set by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, for clarifications purposes, when you say "along the axis set by them," to whom are you referring when you say "them"?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I said a moment ago. Either the commander of the operations group or the corps command who determine the priorities for the attack, and we would be assigned a small portion of that area. Every unit would be assigned a particular area where they were supposed to attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's now break down the time periods a little bit if we can. When you say "operation group," in 1993 what operation are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: In view of the fact that these operations were taking place in the area of Vitez and Novi Travnik, Zabrdzje, this belonged to the Bosanska Krajina Operations Group. So I was referring to them. When we're talking about an operations group, then I mean this one, the Bosnia Krajina Operations Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention, Mr. Awad, to the year 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, before we do that, I'd like the witness to explore a bit more the procedure that was followed when the El Mujahid Detachment went into combat action. I told us that you would be called to the 3rd command -- the 3rd Corps command and be assigned an area for combat and assigned a task and a time and also be told which other units would take part in that attack. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Tell me, what would happen next? Would you -- or would the delegation from the El Mujahid Detachment then just return to Mehurici and -- and start, implement those directives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would first reconnoiter the terrain. Then -- the terrain where the attacks should be carried out. Then we would coordinate with the unit holding the line there, and they would show us terrain because, after all, we don't know the area. Then we would do the reconnaissance, and then we would prepare for the attack. Before the attack a meeting would be held regarding the readiness of units for the attack, and the date would be set for the attack and the method in which it would be carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: A meeting between who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The units taking part and those who determine the priorities, whether it was the corps command or the operations group command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Would the El Mujahid Detachment have an opportunity to decide independently of whether they would wish to join in that action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Mujahedin Detachment is always ready for combat. That is why they had come, to fight. I can't walk around Bosnia and say, "I'm going to attack here, and tomorrow somewhere else." There has to be some sort of order, and one has to respect the host. Before going to his terrain, I have to ask him. So there has to be coordination when an attack is being carried out. So the detachment usually wouldn't be alone. I can't just go and attack somewhere. This was coordinated. The detachment at first wasn't very strong. If we're talking about a hundred men, that's an insignificant number. So it was essential to coordinate with other units. We'd have a small sector for attacking, but we cannot do it alone. When a hundred men enters a forest, a wood, they can cover not even 50 metres, not to mention a kilometre or more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. Were you aware of any instance where the El Mujahid Detachment had to decline from taking part in a combat action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There wasn't refusal outright, but usually if reconnaissance is carried out of the terrain and if the military commander and the reconnaissance people see that we lack the proper elements for an attack, for the attack to be successful -- because an attack is not for the sake of an attack and for people to get killed, but when one attacks, the aim is to succeed, to gain control of the location we are attacking. If you wish -- I think the Prosecutor will come to that later. I think in 1994 -- I can tell you now or later on when the Prosecutor comes to these questions, I will provide the answers. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The reason I'm putting these questions, and we may well get back to them if that is -- is the Prosecution's line, because I do not wish to interfere with it, with the Prosecution, but I need to have now or later an understanding of the way in which the El Mujahid Detachment would -- would cooperate with the ABiH units, and what I was particularly looking for was to know if -- if the El Mujahid Detachment was given -- was given the flexibility of opting out independently and by its own decision of combat actions that were planned. But you can answer now, or you can wait until later. It's -- please answer now, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the El Mujahedin Detachment is concerned, I must repeat once again. People who had come from abroad, they came to assist, not to rest or to have a cup of coffee and to tour the area. They came to fight. Whereas the Bosnians, the men who joined the Arabs, the Mujahedin, they accepted them and wanted to fight with them. And the whole detachment together, the aim of the whole detachment was to assist as much as possible and to liberate as much territory as possible. As for actual opting out or refusal, there weren't cases when anyone said, "I will not attack," but, rather, there would be talks, discussions to explain the situation. There was a case in 1994 when the command of the corps said that the priority of the attack should be at the Vogosca theatre of war, and the detachment, after two successful operations, was transferred to the area of Zavidovici. The terrain was such that it was not possible to attack. Autumn had started. The wood was -- one could see through it. One -- there were no -- there was no foliage to hide behind, no rocks so that could one could reach a trench and do reconnaissance. The configuration of the land was such there were 726, 702, and 706 features, and 726 and 702 and 706, they covered each other, and there was no possibility of approaching them under protection. When there's foliage it's give, never mind when there are no leaves. So the military commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, for instance, the combat operation was postponed, I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't finished. If I may finish first. So in this case, when men did reconnaissance and said that it was not possible to carry out the attack, they told the commander, but the division commander and the corps commander, under pressure of other units that were lying around and who were doing nothing, said, "But you have of to attack." They were full of zeal. They wanted to attack. We said, "That's not a problem for us, but -- we can attack, but we will not succeed. We will just lose men, and we will not capture anything." But the decision was that we had to do the attack for the benefit of the other units. So as to avoid a conflict or a misunderstanding between the El Mujahedin command and the corps and division command, the decision was to carry out a fake attack. Now, what did that mean? We would send -- send mean to reach the line which existed. The 328th Brigade was holding the line and the trenches, and all the commanders said, "We're ready for the attack in the morning." We said, "Fine." Our members were on the line, and they opened fire, but none of the other fighters made any progress. They didn't move forward a single metre. And then they attributed the failure to us. They said that it was the fault of the El Mujahedin, but our command had said that it was not a good occasion, a good opportunity for an attack. Afterwards, about some six months later, the operation was carried out and we alone, without anyone's assistance, except Allah, we managed to take control of these features, though everyone thought that we would need air force support to achieve it, but we achieved it nevertheless, but later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Awad, let's continue talking about -- let's continue talking about this operation that you've just described and then we'll maybe rewind the time clock a little bit, but I do have some follow-up questions based on what you've just told us. The first one, you indicated that this was 1994. Can you be more specific, sir, in terms of what time period in 1994, what month in 1994?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: End of October or early November, but it was autumn in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: It could be late October or early November. Sometime around then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: All right. You've also told us, sir, about some reconnaissance that was done before that operation. Do you recall approximately when that reconnaissance was undertaken?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: When the decision was made to transfer the detachment from the Sarici-Teslici front to the Zavidovici front a group was assigned of scouts who were going to reconnoiter the terrain, and on the first day there was -- the team that carried out the reconnaissance, they tried to carry out reconnaissance in five or six days. We had a 15-day deadline. But in that deadline of 15 days, it was really not possible to approach the enemy positions in order to reconnoiter and to find out more. I think it was in October, in the month of October, when this reconnaissance in that area was conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And this was October 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Awad, you told us that this reconnaissance was undertaken shortly after the detachment moved from the Sarici-Teslic area to Zavidovici area. Who made that decision, sir, to relocate the unit?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The corps commander, like I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us a little bit more about the discussions or meetings that related to this operation in the autumn of 1994?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The detachment command was summoned by the corps command or the corps commander, and they were told that the priority was to attack in the Zavidovici front and to transfer the unit there and to carry out an attack there. A team was established that led us. I was part of that team. It included commander Abu Mali.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the is second name. Probably Muatez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then we came to the team that was in Zavidovici. The commander Hasan greeted us there, and they said that they were eager to receive this unit that had two successes in a row in the Saric-Teslici area. Then there was a team that -- there that was going to guide us, to show us the terrain, and people were assigned to follow our scouts, to show them the terrain. So the division commander gave some men to us to show us around. After we spoke, we went out into the field, and we carried out reconnaissance there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But let me just interrupt you there for one moment. When you say the division commander, can you tell us please what division and the name of the division commander?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Fadil Hasanagic. I said the name. And it was the 35th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, approximately when this meeting that you've been telling us took place in Zavidovici, when Commander Hasanagic basically facilitated this reconnaissance?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I don't know the exact -- the exact date in October 1994. After receiving notification that the detachment had to transfer to the Zavidovici area and when we got to the division, immediately a team was assigned to follow us or escort us. There were people there who were entrusted with coordination. They took us to the field, and then other scouts were assigned to be with our scouts to show them the terrain. The next day -- I can't remember the exact date, but this was as soon as we transferred to Zavidovici. We immediately embarked on this reconnaissance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And approximately how long did that reconnaissance take?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: We were given 15 days for the preparations, but I could say that we spent about seven days in reconnaissance, walking around. People were trying to find away of getting closer, but there was no possibility for that, and I think even before that time expired we reported back that the attack could not be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to ask you about that particular aspect. When you say "we reported back," to whom did you report that the operation would not be successful?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The corps commander and the division commander were at the meeting, and it was said -- we informed the corps commander that the attack could not be carried out. However, they insisted. He insisted that the attack must be carried out because of the other units and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Awad, I need as much precision as possible. So when you say "the corps commander," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The corps commander at the time was General Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, at this point in time, October 1994, who was the division commander that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Which division?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe you said earlier you reported to back to the 3rd Corps commander and the 35th Division commander. You've just told us at that time General Mahmuljin was the commander of the 3rd Corps. At that point in time, October 1994, who was the 35th Division commander?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Fadil Hasanagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After this meeting where you reported that this task was not possible due to the time of year and the topography, how much time elapsed before that attack was carried out, this false attack as you put it earlier?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: It wasn't that much time. If we know that the last operation in the Teslic front was carried out in October, early October, then we can say that -- I said the end of October. Fifteen days from the time we were received by Hasanagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in that intervening short period of time, were there any other meetings between the commander of the El Mujahedin Detachment and the 35th Division and/or the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: There were no more meetings. The first meeting was a separate meeting at the corps command when we were told that the detachment had to transfer. There was an encounter at the division command, at Fadil Hasanagic's. After that, there was one when we informed them. However, there were two meetings more. The last meeting was when all the commanders of other units were summoned who insisted on their readiness to execute the attack, and at that time it was decided that the attack must be carried out. And then in the evening or on the following day -- or I think it was the same evening, a meeting was held - I think it was at the panorama in Zavidovici - where all laid the blame on the El Mujahedin for failure, but they did not themselves fire a single bullet. And then Fadil Hasanagic angrily at that point thought that we were pretending, that we did not wish to carry out the attack even though we explained. He responded angrily, "You will stay with me still." I mean, it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Mr. Awad, I want to return to the topic of Sarici and Teslic, which you've mentioned several times. Can you tell us a little bit about the time period in which those operations occurred?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I think that the first operation, the attack on Pisana Jelika and Visoko Glava was carried out in late August or early September. The second attack at the Brdo facility was carried out in October, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In which year, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, these two operations in this area of Sarici and Teslic were prior to the unit moving to Zavidovici; is that correct? Okay.

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let's just return to that time period, though, because we -- we kind of skipped ahead to talk about the autumn 1994 operation that you've been talking about. So I want to go -- focus your attention now back to these earlier operations in the Sarici-Teslic area. Can you tell us, Mr. Awad, how it came to be that the detachment was operating in that area, Sarici, Teslic, in late summer, early autumn 1994?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The detachment was billeted in that area. They were holding the line towards a place that was called. Karanovac. We received notification that it would be good to reconnoiter the terrain and clear that facility that was called Pisana Jelika and Visoko Glava. I think that some other units were supposed to participate in that with us, but Muatez and the others, the other experts in the detachment, decided that we would attack alone, without anyone's assistance, because we were afraid that somebody would not come through on the left or the right flank and then we would be left, because the terrain was such that you really couldn't do it one by one, because both facilities, Pisana Jelika and Visoko Glava, had to be attacked simultaneously. So that's how we got the recommendation to attack both places. We were summoned to a conversation when we were told that it would be a good thing to do an action on those two places, and then after the meeting it was decided that it would be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. I would like to try to finish this topic before we break for the day, so if you could just bear with me a couple more questions, Mr. Awad. This -- this meeting -- this meeting that you've told us about, when and where did this meeting take place, and who attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly when this was held at the corps command and how this whole task happened. I wasn't there when the assignment or task was given. Later, I think a meeting was held in the 3 North Operations Group where the actions were coordinated. I don't recall that there was a meeting at the corps command where this was discussed. Perhaps it was, but I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, at this time period, late summer, early autumn 1994, what the relationship was between the El Mujahedin Detachment and Operation Group 3 North?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The relations were good. We were formally resubordinated to the 3 North Operations Group, and we cooperated with the commander. I think his name was Musim [phoen] Begovic. And we need to state this right at the beginning that we or the detachment command didn't trust all the commanders. We mostly -- the commander that we trusted the most was the commander of the 3rd Corps, Sakib Mahmuljin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just ask you this question, sir: When you say you were formally resubordinated to OG 3 North, I would like to ask or would like you to tell us, if you can, who made that decision. Who resubordinated Odred El Mujahedin to OG 3 North?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The corps commander, because the El Mujahedin Detachment is an independent unit that was directly under the command of the 3rd Corps. That's how it was for that unit. So the corps commander made the decision for the unit to be resubordinated to the OG 3 North group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am aware of the time. I had one exhibit I'd like to show the witness concerning events in 1994 that relate to this and then that will be the end of 1994, and then we could just start tomorrow with 1995. If I could beg the Court and the interpreters' indulgence. I would ask now that the witness be shown the document P01810, P01810.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Awad, do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear you, sir. Do you have the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: I have several documents, but, yes, I have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to draw your attention, sir, to the numbered paragraph 1 under the word "Order."

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, what this is all about, this reference to Pioneer Squads or Pioneer Squad?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: These are the de-miners which belong to the winter unit that belongs to the 3rd Corps. They helped us. These people would usually be attached to us to remove mines before the attack. Before any attack they would dismantle the mines that they had laid down before, or the unit that would be holding that territory had laid down before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you now look, sir, at the numbered paragraph 3, and can you perhaps comment upon this part of the order that requires the detachment to provide accommodation and food to the Pioneer Squad and to arm them with automatic weapons?

utterances.speaker: AJMAN AWAD
utterances.text: The Pioneers were staying in the area where the detachment was billeted at Karanovac, in the Karanovci area, and they had been given a tent where they slept at Karanovac where they were billeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Awad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution would ask that this document P01810 be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That is Exhibit 1128, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I am grateful for the extra time. This would be a perfect spot for us to adjourn for the day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we do that and because I may forget, can I ask you just one little point of explanation, sir. You mentioned when you were planning -- when you talked about an attack that you were planning to do alone as the El Mujahedin because you were not sure whether the others would come along, did that attack take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it was undertaken by the El Mujahedin alone. What was the strength of the El Mujahedin during that attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe 2 to 300 men, not more. We're talking about 1994. That was the time that the unit was larger. It was no longer made up of a hundred men but included Bosniaks who had joined the El Mujahedin Detachment. So the unit was larger. The two facilities were attacked in 17 minutes, something that the two brigades couldn't capture. That's what was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take an adjournment, and we'll reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
